title: Relevant, sufficient and credible evidence; strengthen or weaken
blurb: Judge whether evidence is relevant, sufficient and credible, and pick the new fact that would most strengthen or weaken an argument.
question: An energy-drink company claims its product raises test scores, citing its own study of 20 employees and its CEO's praise. A TEAS item asks which new fact, if true, would most weaken the claim. One option says the drink is popular with college students. Why is that not the answer?

teach.h: Evaluate the support, not the claim
teach.body: To evaluate an argument, test its evidence and reasoning. Evidence should be relevant (actually about the claim), sufficient (enough of it, not one anecdote) and credible (from a reliable, current, unbiased source), and the reasoning that links it to the claim should be valid. In plain English: is it on point, is there enough of it, can you trust where it came from, and does it really lead to the conclusion?

head: Test
Ask
Fails when
rows: One story or a tiny sample
Does it lead to the claim?

teach.body: FocusFuel energy drink raises test scores. In a study paid for by our company, 20 of our own employees drank FocusFuel for a week and then scored higher on a word puzzle than they had the week before. Our CEO, a former college track star, says FocusFuel gives him an edge every morning. Students across the country are already making the switch.

teach.caption: The students line is bandwagon pressure: popularity is not proof.

items: Find the claim and the evidence offered for it.
Name the gap: what must be true for the evidence to prove the claim? (That the drink, not something else, raised the scores.)
To STRENGTHEN, choose the fact that closes the gap: a larger controlled study, or ruling out another cause.
To WEAKEN, choose the fact that opens it: another explanation, a flaw in the sample or a biased source.

teach.h: 'If true' means accept it, then test it
teach.body: Strengthen and weaken items say 'which of the following, if true'. Accept each option as true; your job is to judge its effect on the link between evidence and claim. An option that merely repeats the claim adds nothing. An option that is true but about a different issue (the drink's flavor, its price) does nothing. The right option changes how much the evidence actually proves.

teach.text: Classic wrong answers: an option that restates the claim ('FocusFuel really does work'), an accurate fact that is irrelevant (it comes in three flavors), and a vivid anecdote offered as strong proof. Also avoid judging by whether you agree: evaluate the support, not the position.

teach.body: Priya Shah, applying to a pharmacy technician program, must pick the fact that most weakens the FocusFuel claim. 'FocusFuel is popular with college students' is irrelevant to whether it works. 'FocusFuel contains caffeine' does not undermine anything. 'The employees had practiced the same type of puzzle during the week' gives another reason scores rose, so the drink may have done nothing. She picks it: it opens a gap between evidence and claim.

items: Relevant: about this claim. Sufficient: enough of it. Credible: trustworthy source.
Another possible cause weakens a causal claim; ruling it out strengthens it.
A larger controlled study strengthens; a tiny or seller-funded study is weaker.
Options that restate the claim or add irrelevant facts do not strengthen.
Judge the support, not whether you agree with the conclusion.

summary: You can now test evidence for relevance, sufficiency and credibility and spot reasoning that leaves another cause open. You can also choose the new fact that would most strengthen or weaken an argument.

A.q:
Read the passage.

Our town should ban gas-powered leaf blowers. Last fall, my neighbor ran his blower every Saturday at 7 a.m., and it woke my whole family. No one should have to put up with that kind of noise.

Which statement best describes the main weakness of the evidence?
options: It comes from a source with a financial interest in the ban.
It is out of date because it describes last fall's events.
It rests on one neighbor's habits, too little to support a ban.
It is about leaf blowers, while the claim is about all noise.
A.why: The only evidence is one neighbor's behavior. A single anecdote is not sufficient to justify a town-wide ban.

whyNot.0: Nothing suggests the writer would profit from a ban.
whyNot.1: Last fall is recent; the problem is how little evidence there is, not its age.
whyNot.3: The claim is specifically about leaf blowers, so the evidence is on topic.

A.q:
Read the passage.

Teenagers need more sleep on school nights. A recent survey found that adults who sleep seven to nine hours report better moods than adults who sleep less.

What is the main problem with the evidence?
options: It is about adults, while the claim is about teenagers.
It comes from a survey, which cannot be used as evidence.
It is too old to apply to teenagers living today.
It comes from a source that sells sleep products.
A.why: The claim is about teenagers, but the evidence describes adults. Evidence about a different group is not directly relevant.

whyNot.1: Surveys can be valid evidence; the issue is who was surveyed.
whyNot.2: The passage calls the survey recent.
whyNot.3: The passage says nothing about who ran the survey.

A.q: A website claims that a new pillow cures neck pain. Its evidence is a study showing that 9 of 10 users felt better after a month. Which fact about the study would most reduce its credibility?
options: The study was led by a university sleep researcher.
The study was paid for by the pillow's maker.
The study lasted one month rather than one full year.
The study was described in plain language for readers.
A.why: A study funded by the seller of the product has a conflict of interest, which undermines its credibility.

whyNot.0: A qualified, university-based researcher would add to the study's credibility, not reduce it.
whyNot.2: A month is short, but this is about sufficiency, not source credibility, and it is the smaller problem.
whyNot.3: Plain language does not make a study less reliable.

B.q:
Read the passage.

After Oakdale Middle School added a 20-minute recess after lunch, afternoon behavior referrals dropped by 30 percent. The recess clearly improved student behavior.

Which of the following, if true, would most WEAKEN the argument?
options: Students at Oakdale said they enjoyed the new recess.
Teachers at Oakdale also supported adding the recess.
Oakdale hired two counselors the same semester.
The recess was held outdoors when weather allowed.
B.why: New counselors arriving at the same time offer another explanation for fewer referrals. The drop may not be due to recess at all.

whyNot.0: Students' enjoyment does not affect whether recess caused the drop.
whyNot.1: Teacher support says nothing about what caused the change in behavior.
whyNot.3: Where recess was held does not challenge the link between recess and behavior.

B.q:
Read the passage.

A small study of 30 adults found that those who took a daily ten-minute walk after dinner had lower blood sugar the next morning. The author concludes that short walks after meals help control blood sugar.

Which of the following, if true, would most STRENGTHEN the conclusion?
options: Many adults say they enjoy walking after their evening meal.
Walking is one of the most popular forms of exercise in the US.
The 30 adults in the study all lived in the same small town.
A study of 2,000 adults with a non-walking group found the same.
B.why: A much larger study with a comparison group that did not walk, reaching the same result, makes the evidence more sufficient and rules out chance.

whyNot.0: Enjoyment says nothing about blood sugar.
whyNot.1: Popularity is irrelevant to whether walking lowers blood sugar.
whyNot.2: A narrow sample from one town makes the evidence weaker, not stronger.

B.q:
Read the passage.

The city's new bus app has reduced waiting times at stops. Since the app launched, riders report waiting an average of six minutes instead of eleven.

Which of the following, if true, would NOT strengthen the argument?
options: Bus schedules and routes were unchanged when the app launched.
The city's bus app is easy to use and free to download.
Riders who use the app wait less than riders who do not.
GPS data from the buses confirm the shorter wait times.
B.why: Being easy to use and free says nothing about whether the app actually reduced waiting times. It is true but irrelevant to the claim.

whyNot.0: Ruling out schedule changes removes another explanation, which strengthens the claim.
whyNot.2: A comparison between app users and non-users supports the app as the cause.
whyNot.3: Independent GPS data make the rider reports more credible.

C.q:
Read the passage.

In March, Linden County installed a traffic light at the intersection of Route 9 and Mill Road. Crashes at the intersection fell from 14 in the previous year to 4 in the year after. The traffic light made the intersection safer.

Which of the following, if true, would most WEAKEN the argument?
options: Drivers in Linden County say the light makes them feel safer.
The light was installed after residents signed a petition.
Crashes also fell at two other spots where lights were added.
Route 9 was closed for repairs for eight months of that year.
C.why: If Route 9 was closed for most of the year, far less traffic passed through the intersection, which could explain the drop without the light.

whyNot.0: Feeling safer is not evidence about the actual crash numbers.
whyNot.1: How the light came to be installed does not affect whether it reduced crashes.
whyNot.2: Similar drops where lights were newly added support the idea that lights reduce crashes, so this strengthens the argument rather than weakening it.

C.q:
Read the passage.

Patients at Hillside Clinic who received a reminder phone call kept 92 percent of their appointments, compared with 78 percent for patients who received no call. Reminder calls improve attendance.

Which of the following, if true, would most STRENGTHEN the argument?
options: The clinic chose at random which patients would get calls.
Patients who got calls had more appointments overall.
The clinic staff who made the calls had years of training.
Most patients at the clinic prefer calls to text messages.
C.why: If patients were assigned to get calls at random, the two groups should be alike in other ways, ruling out the possibility that more reliable patients simply got the calls.

whyNot.1: More appointments overall does not show the calls caused better attendance.
whyNot.2: Staff experience is not evidence that calls changed attendance.
whyNot.3: A preference between calls and texts does not bear on whether calls work.

C.q: A student wants to support the claim that the school's new tutoring center has improved math grades. Which evidence would be the most relevant and sufficient?
options: A comment from one student who says tutoring helped her a lot
Grades of 300 students before and after using the tutoring center
A list of the tutoring center's hours and the subjects it covers
A statement from the principal that the center is a great success
C.why: Grades for hundreds of students before and after tutoring measure the exact outcome in the claim, with a large sample.

whyNot.0: One student's comment is an anecdote: relevant but not sufficient.
whyNot.2: Hours and subjects describe the center but say nothing about grades.
whyNot.3: The principal's opinion is not data about grades and may be biased.

reteach.title: Think of online product reviews
reteach.question: You are choosing a blender online. One has a single five-star review from the seller's cousin; another has 2,000 reviews from verified buyers. Why do you trust the second one more?

blocks.body: A review about the blender's shipping box is not relevant to how it blends. One review is not sufficient; 2,000 are. A review written by the seller's cousin is not credible; reviews from verified buyers are. Learning that the five-star ratings came only from people who got free blenders would weaken your trust; learning that buyers who paid full price rate it just as highly would strengthen it.

blocks.text: A review saying 'This blender is great because it is a great blender' adds nothing. Restating the claim is not evidence.

explain.body: Relevant evidence is about the exact claim: the same group, the same outcome, the same situation. Evidence about adults does not prove a claim about teens; evidence about a puzzle does not prove a claim about test scores.

test.q: An author claims that the city's new bike lanes have reduced car traffic downtown. Which evidence is most relevant?
options: Bike sales at downtown shops have risen this year.
Car counts downtown fell after the lanes opened.
Most residents say they support more bike lanes.
The lanes were painted green to improve safety.
test.why: The claim is about car traffic downtown, so counts of cars downtown before and after the lanes measure the exact outcome.

whyNot.0: Bike sales do not show whether car traffic fell.
whyNot.2: Public support is an opinion, not a measure of traffic.
whyNot.3: The color of the lanes says nothing about car traffic.

explain.body: Sufficient evidence is enough to support the size of the claim. One story or a handful of cases cannot support a claim about a whole town, school or population.

test.q: A writer claims that most nursing students in the state prefer online classes. Which evidence would best meet the test of sufficiency?
options: A survey of 1,500 students at 20 nursing programs
Interviews with the writer's three nursing classmates
A blog post by one nursing student who likes online classes
A quote from a teacher who enjoys teaching online
test.why: A survey of 1,500 students across 20 programs is large and varied enough to support a claim about most students in the state.

whyNot.1: Three classmates from one program are far too few to represent the state.
whyNot.2: One student's blog post is an anecdote.
whyNot.3: A teacher's preference is not evidence of what students prefer.

explain.body: Credible evidence comes from a reliable, current, unbiased source: a qualified expert, an independent study, a government health agency. A seller funding research on its own product has a conflict of interest.

test.q: An article about the safety of a new allergy medicine cites four sources. Which is the most credible?
options: A blog by a parent whose child took the medicine
A press release from the medicine's manufacturer
A celebrity's social media post praising the drug
A recent independent study in a medical journal
test.why: A recent, independent, published study has no conflict of interest and reflects expert research, making it the most credible.

whyNot.0: One parent's experience is an anecdote, not expert evidence.
whyNot.1: The manufacturer profits from the drug, a conflict of interest.
whyNot.2: A celebrity is not a medical authority.

explain.body: To strengthen, add support or rule out another cause. To weaken, show another cause could explain the result, or reveal a flaw in the sample or source. Options that restate the claim or add unrelated facts do neither.

test.q:
Read the passage.

Since Pine Valley Hospital began offering free parking for visitors, patient satisfaction scores have risen. Free parking made patients more satisfied.

Which of the following, if true, would most WEAKEN the argument?
options: Visitors said free parking saved them money each week.
The parking lot was resurfaced the year before the change.
The hospital opened a new wing with private rooms that year.
Free parking is offered at several other local hospitals.
test.why: A new wing of private rooms is another plausible cause of higher satisfaction, so free parking may not explain the rise.

whyNot.0: Saving money shows visitors liked the change, which does not challenge the claim.
whyNot.1: A change made the year before does not explain the later rise.
whyNot.3: What other hospitals offer does not affect what caused the change at Pine Valley.
